topic: hallmarks: mitochondria, senescence and stem cells
question: Besides being the cell's powerhouses, what do mitochondria act as that can trigger inflammation and cell death?
answers: Latent triggers of inflammation and cell death
Triggers of inflammation (when ROS or mtDNA leak out) and cell death (when lethal enzymes are released)

receipt.quote:
Mitochondria are not only the powerhouses of the cell but also constitute latent triggers of inflammation (when reactive oxygen species [ROS] or mtDNA leak out of the organelle causing activa-
tion of inflammasomes or cytosolic DNA sensors, respectively) and cell death (when activators of caspases, nucleases, or other lethal enzymes are released from the intermembrane space).

topic: hallmarks: mitochondria, senescence and stem cells
question: Why does ageing compromise mitochondrial function? Name one mechanism.
answers: Deficient proteostasis destabilizing respiratory chain complexes

receipt.quote:
With aging, mitochondrial function deteriorates due to multiple in-
tertwined mechanisms including the accumulation of mtDNA mu-
tations, deficient proteostasis leading to the destabilization of res-
piratory chain complexes, reduced turnover of the organelle, and
changes in mitochondrial dynamics.

question: What are senolytics?
answers: Small chemical compounds that selectively kill senescent cells

receipt.quote:
The strong association between cellular senescence and multiple
pathologies has spurred the search for small chemical compounds
that selectively kill senescent cells and that are referred to as ‘‘se-
nolytics.230’’

question: What is the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) usually doing to tissue in many diseases?
answers: Causing chronic inflammation and progressive fibrosis

receipt.quote: In many diseases, the net effect of SASP is chronic inflammation and progressive ﬁbrosis.228

topic: hallmarks: mitochondria, senescence and stem cells
question: Why does navitoclax kill senescent cells?
answers: Senescent cells depend on BCL2-family proteins (BCLXL, BCL2, BCLW) to resist apoptosis, and navitoclax targets all three

receipt.quote:
The survival and
apoptotic resistance of senescent cells strongly depends on the
BCL2 family of proteins, specially BCLXL, but also BCL2 and
BCLW. This renders senescent cells highly vulnerable to navito-
clax, which targets these three proteins.

question: What is the most compelling evidence that cellular senescence causes ageing, and in which species?
answers: Continued genetic or pharmacological elimination of senescent cells extends healthspan and longevity in naturally aged mice

receipt.quote:
The most compelling evidence for the causal role of cellular senescence in aging is that continued genetic or pharma-
cological elimination of senescent cells extends the healthspan
and longevity of naturally aged mice.59

question: According to the review, when does cellular senescence become pathological rather than helpful for tissue repair?
answers: When immune clearance of senescent cells fails, so they accumulate and their SASP causes fibrosis

receipt.quote:
The patholog-
ical consequences of senescence only become visible when
the second step of immune clearance is not achieved, and the
accumulation of senescent cells and the SASP effects on the tis-
sue microenvironment eventually result in ﬁbrosis.

topic: hallmarks: mitochondria, senescence and stem cells
question: Why does ageing make mitochondria work worse, and what does that do to the cell?
answers: mtDNA mutations build up, proteostasis is deficient and turnover is reduced. Energy supply is compromised, ROS production rises, and membrane leakiness can cause inflammation and cell death.

receipt.quote:
With aging, mitochondrial function deteriorates due to multiple in-
tertwined mechanisms including the accumulation of mtDNA mu-
tations, deﬁcient proteostasis leading to the destabilization of res-
piratory chain complexes, reduced turnover of the organelle, and
changes in mitochondrial dynamics. This situation compromises
the contribution of mitochondria to cellular bioenergetics, en-
hances the production of ROS, and may trigger accidental perme-
abilization of mitochondrial membranes causing inﬂammation and
cell death.

topic: hallmarks: mitochondria, senescence and stem cells
question: What is "mitohormesis", and under what conditions does it extend lifespan in model organisms?
answers: Compromising mitochondrial function can paradoxically improve lifespan by inducing a hormetic response, provided the inhibition is partial and occurs early in development.

receipt.quote:
Paradoxically, in model organisms, lifespan can
be improved by compromising mitochondrial function, which in-
duces a hormetic response (‘‘mitohormesis’’), provided that this
inhibition is partial and occurs early during development.
